content: The Fallopian tubes, also referred to as oviducts, uterine tubes, or salpinges (singular: salpinx), are two slender tubular structures that connect the ovaries to the uterus in female mammals. These tubes are essential components of the female reproductive system. Each Fallopian tube is attached to the cornual end of the uterus on either side and extends toward an ovary, ending in a structure called the fimbria. The fimbria is a fringe-like structure that helps guide the ovum into the tube. Importantly, the Fallopian tubes are not directly connected to the ovaries but open into the peritoneal cavity, which is the internal abdominal space. This anatomical arrangement creates a direct communication pathway between the peritoneal cavity and the external environment via the vagina. In humans, the length of the Fallopian tubes typically ranges from 7 to 14 centimeters. The Fallopian tube is divided into four distinct regions, each with specific roles: 1. Infundibulum: This region contains the fimbria and is closest to the ovary. 2. Ampulla: This is the widest section of the tube and is the most common site of fertilization. 3. Isthmus: A narrower segment of the tube. 4. Intramural oviduct: This portion is embedded within the wall of the uterus. The histological structure of the Fallopian tube consists of three layers: 1. Mucosa: This inner layer is characterized by distinctive folds, which are most elaborate in the ampulla and nearly absent in the intramural portion. The mucosa contains two types of cells: ciliated cells, which help move the ovum, and peg cells, which secrete nutrients. 2. Muscularis externa: This middle layer is composed of smooth muscle that aids in the movement of the ovum through peristaltic contractions. 3. Serosa: This is the outermost layer, which provides structural support. The Fallopian tubes are highly mobile structures. Time-lapse imaging has shown that they move dynamically within the pelvis, often crossing over to the opposite side or lying on top of the uterus, depending on the phase of the menstrual cycle. During ovulation, an ovum matures within an ovarian follicle. When the follicle ruptures, the ovum is released into the peritoneal cavity and is captured by the fimbria of the Fallopian tube. The ovum then travels through the tube toward the uterus, propelled by the coordinated movement of cilia lining the mucosa. This journey can take several hours to days. If fertilization occurs within the Fallopian tube, the resulting zygote typically implants in the uterine endometrium, initiating pregnancy. However, in some cases, the embryo may implant within the Fallopian tube itself, leading to an ectopic pregnancy, also known as a tubal pregnancy. From an embryological perspective, the Fallopian tubes develop from the Müllerian ducts in female embryos. These ducts also give rise to the uterus and the upper portion of the vagina. In male embryos, the Müllerian ducts regress, and the Wolffian ducts develop into structures such as the epididymis and vas deferens. The Fallopian tubes are not homologous to any male reproductive structures. Pathological conditions affecting the Fallopian tubes include pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), which can lead to obstruction of the tubes. This obstruction may result in infertility or increase the risk of ectopic pregnancy. Surgical procedures involving the Fallopian tubes include: Salpingectomy: The removal of one Fallopian tube. Bilateral salpingectomy: The removal of both Fallopian tubes. Salpingo-oophorectomy: The removal of a Fallopian tube along with at least one ovary. Tuboplasty: A surgical procedure to restore patency to an obstructed Fallopian tube. The Fallopian tubes are named after Gabriele Falloppio, a 16th-century Italian anatomist who first described them. While the term Fallopian is eponymous, it is often written in lowercase as fallopian in modern English usage. The Greek term salpinx (σαλπιγξ), meaning trumpet, reflects the tube's shape.
